title: Eating disorders before, during and after pregnancy | NHS inform
text:
Eating disorders before, during and after pregnancy
Eating disorders
are serious mental health conditions. Someone with an eating disorder will regularly eat too much or too little. They’ll also spend a lot of time thinking about food and their weight or body shape.
Eating disorders can have a significant impact on health, wellbeing and relationships. They can also affect your health in pregnancy and how your baby develops.
Read more about eating disorders
Let your midwife and GP know if you’re pregnant and have an eating disorder, or have had one in the past. Tell your health visitor when you meet them too.
This means everyone involved in your care can give you the best advice and support. They’ll make sure your pregnancy and baby are as healthy as possible.
Eating disorders and fertility
Eating disorders can affect fertility. Some eating disorders can make it harder to conceive. This is because of changes in your body and your hormones.
However, you can still become pregnant when you have an eating disorder, even if you’re not having regular periods.
You should still use contraception if you do not want to become pregnant.
Planning a pregnancy
It can be helpful to discuss planning a pregnancy with your GP practice or mental health team, if you have one, if you have:
an eating disorder
had an eating disorder in the past
They can help you plan and access the right support.
Your GP may do some tests to check your health.
How eating disorders might affect you during pregnancy
Having an eating disorder during pregnancy can increase the chance of:
miscarriage
complications during childbirth
gestational diabetes
low energy or fainting
poor nutrition and dehydration
problems with your heart
high blood pressure
breastfeeding
challenges
Having an eating disorder can also affect your baby:
not growing as they should (fetal growth restriction)
being born early (preterm birth)
having a low birth weight
If you have an eating disorder you have a higher risk of getting
postnatal depression
.
Your healthcare team can reduce the risk of complications by providing you with support and monitoring.
Risks of developing an eating disorder during pregnancy
If you’ve had an eating disorder before, you might be more likely to experience a relapse of your eating disorder during pregnancy.
This might be because you :
feel out of control as your body changes quickly
worry about gaining weight
hear people commenting on your changing size and weight
have sickness during pregnancy
want to avoid certain foods
have a bigger appetite or cravings which might cause binges
have gestational diabetes which means checking your blood sugar levels and controlling your diet
If you recognise early signs that the symptoms of an
eating disorder
are returning, speak to your GP practice and midwife.
Eating disorders after having a baby
An eating disorder might develop or reappear after you have a baby because of:
body image worries
perceived pressure from society to bounce back and lose weight
postnatal depression
,
anxiety
or
stress
changes in routine which might mean eating at unusual times
lack of sleep
breastfeeding which might make you feel hungrier or mean you need to eat more calories
traumatic birth
relationship changes and social isolation
If you recognise that the symptoms of an
eating disorder
are returning, speak to your GP practice, midwife or health visitor.
How an eating disorder can affect breastfeeding
Pressure to lose weight can sometimes lead to behaviours like over exercising or dieting. If you choose to breastfeed, your body will need extra energy and nutrients to support your milk supply.
It’s important to look after your own health, nutrition and wellbeing. Eating regular meals and snacks will help your recovery from birth and help your body provide breastmilk. Try to stay well hydrated by drinking plenty water. It’s also important to rest when you can too.
If you’d like advice about breastfeeding, speak to your:
midwife
health visitor
local breastfeeding support group
Visit Parent Club for more breastfeeding information and support
Talking to your family and friends
Having support from your family and friends can be really helpful. Speak to them about what they can do to help you stay well after your baby is born.
It can be helpful to tell your closest family and friends about your eating disorder. You can let them know about:
what symptoms you’ve had in the past
what signs they should look out for
if you take any medication
You could let them know that they can speak to your GP practice, midwife or health visitor if they’re worried about you. They could also speak to your care team for information and advice about eating disorders and how to get support for themselves.
If you can’t or don’t want to talk to your family or friends, you can reach out to other services for support. You can talk to
Breathing Space
if you need someone to talk to.
Beat
also has a helpline you can call for information and advice.
Organisations like
Beat
and
SupportED
can offer support to people with an eating disorder and their families and carers.
How family and friends can help you
You could ask your family and friends to help you with things like:
cooking healthy nutritious meals for you
helping with household chores like cleaning and doing dishes
spending time with the baby while you take a break or have a bath or shower
Tommy’s have a pregnancy and post-birth wellbeing plan
that can help you think about support you might need.
Read more about how to support someone with an eating disorder
Treatment for eating disorders during pregnancy and when breastfeeding
With all eating disorders, the first step is recognising that there’s a problem and being willing to seek help.
If you’re worried that you have an eating disorder, speak to your GP practice as soon as you can.
It can be very hard to admit that you have a problem and ask for help. You may feel scared but its important to get this help as soon as possible. You could bring a friend or loved one with you to your appointment.
You should be offered the same therapies for eating disorders during pregnancy as other people. Depending on the type of eating disorder, you might be offered:
guided self-help
talking therapies like cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
Read more about eating disorders
Medication for eating disorders during pregnancy and breastfeeding
Whether to continue medication during pregnancy or breastfeeding can vary from person to person.
If you become pregnant or are planning a pregnancy, don’t stop taking your medication suddenly. You can discuss this with your healthcare professional and they can talk to you about potential benefits and risks. You can decide together how best to progress.
